name: PT Bayan Resources Tbk.

frontmatter.title: Bayan Resources: a first-quartile thermal producer priced for a war premium that never ends
frontmatter.summary: A low-cost, net-cash, high-payout Indonesian thermal-coal pure play whose shares still trade far above a life-of-asset value struck at the deck's through-cycle benchmark. This refresh corrects the licence and royalty basis from the annual report, holds volume and costs at the last actual in real terms, and re-mirrors the scenarios; we maintain SELL with a target of Rp4,156 against a price of Rp10,750.
thesis: Through-cycle value is well below the price: a full life-of-asset DCF at the deck's long-run Newcastle marker, with no terminal value, supports Rp3,954 a share against Rp10,750 traded [S0].
The market is capitalising a war premium and a dividend that cannot both persist: the price implies the benchmark near US$205/t through the horizon, far above the deck's long-run path [S0].

The franchise itself is genuinely good — first-quartile cash costs, a net-cash balance sheet and a long reserve life — which is why we are cautious rather than negative on the asset, only on the entry price [S6, S8].

Governance is the live risk flag: control-block holders transferred stock off-market on a PJBS formula at a price well below the tape, PT Jhonlin Baratama emerged with 30.2% of the register, and the exchange sought a clarification while the RKAB process ran alongside [S2, S10].
A dividend-led re-rating is the bull case; a normalising benchmark with an unchanged payout is the bear case, and the two are roughly symmetric in probability [S8].

blocks.text: This is a refresh triggered by the engine re-run and the most-likely policy, and it changes four things. First, the licence and royalty basis is corrected: the annual report shows Bayan mines under coal contracts of work, or CCoW, as well as IUP licences, so the applicable royalty is the contract rate rather than the converter step table the initiation implied — but the rate we book is still the effective rate the accounts show being paid, which is why the target moves little on this point [S6]. Second, volume is now held flat rather than faded after the ramp, because nothing in the reserve statement or the contracted book sources a decline [S6, S8]. Third, sustaining capex per tonne and the payout ratio are held flat in real terms, removing two unexplained drifts. Fourth, the scenarios are re-mirrored on the sector deck's own default shocks, so the bear and bull now move the same four drivers — benchmark, volume, required return and royalty — by mirrored or explicitly sourced amounts, and the bull now carries the volume ramp the company's own stated target supports rather than a token step [S0, S6]. We also carry a small governance overhang in the base cost of equity, not only in the bear [S2, S10, S13]. The rating and the shape of the conclusion are unchanged.

We maintain our coverage of Bayan Resources at SELL with a twelve-month target of Rp4,156, implying a total return of -56.4% from the last close of Rp10,750 [S0]. The company is an unusually clean thermal-coal producer: it mines low-cost sub-bituminous coal in East and South Kalimantan, sells a quarter of its tonnes into the Indonesian domestic market, and has run a net-cash balance sheet with a five-year average payout of 73.0% of profit [S6, S8]. None of that is in dispute. What is in dispute is the price the market now pays for it.

Our primary method is a life-of-asset discounted cash flow that runs over the stated JORC reserve base and stops when the coal is mined out, with no terminal value [S9]. Struck at the sector deck's through-cycle Newcastle marker, and with the realisation haircut the method card requires of an Indonesian producer selling below the Australian marker, it supports Rp3,954 a share [S0]. That is well below the traded price, and it is the single most important number in this report. The two cross-checks we use to stress that conclusion now part company: the exit-multiple cross-check lands close to the reserve DCF, while the dividend-yield anchor sits far above both — and all three sit below the price, which is what section four explains.

The market, in our reading, is not valuing the reserve life at all. It is valuing a dividend stream at a very low yield and a benchmark that reflects a war premium rather than a marginal-cost floor [S0]. Our reverse-DCF work says the current price requires the benchmark to hold near US$205/t through the forecast horizon, a level above even the current premium spot rather than the deck's long-run path [S0]. We are therefore cautious on the entry price, not on the company.

Thermal coal is the workhorse fuel of Asian electricity generation, and Indonesia is the largest
seaborne exporter of it. Producers in the region sell on a mix of index-linked and fixed-price
contracts, with domestic obligations layered on top of export sales. Prices are set globally but
realisations differ by calorific value, ash and sulphur content, and by distance to the importing
market.

Bayan Resources is a thermal-coal producer with mining and infrastructure operations concentrated in Kalimantan, Indonesia [S6]. The group sells unwashed and washed thermal coal and operates its own hauling, barging and port-loading chain, which is unusual among Indonesian producers and is central to its cost position [S8]. In the most recent full year the company produced 68.0 Mt and sold 70.8 Mt of coal, a record for the group and a function of both a large-volume year and the drawdown of stockpiles built in the prior period [S6].

The revenue model is a single dominant line — thermal coal — with a small non-coal tail in plantations and services that is immaterial to group value [S6]. Because the company reports in US dollars, its revenue and costs are largely currency-matched: coal is sold in dollars and the bulk of its mining, hauling and barging inputs are contracted in dollars or in rupiah at rates that reprice slowly [S8]. That natural hedge is a genuine advantage for a producer whose costs are domestic and whose revenues are export-linked [S8].

The realised price is the swing variable in the model. Bayan's product is lower-calorific-value sub-bituminous coal: the company disclosed that 67.2 Mt was committed for the current year at an average calorific value of 4,088 kcal/kg GAR [S8], roughly a third below the 6,000 kcal/kg NAR benchmark the Newcastle marker is priced at, and consistent with the method card's prescription that an Indonesian producer realises off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle. The modelled long-run realisation ratio of 45% of the Newcastle marker is the arithmetic of that grade discount and the DMO-capped domestic share, calibrated back through the reported realisations of US$48.4/t and US$61.3/t [S6, S8]. Structurally, the discount is a function of coal quality and the tax regime rather than of company execution [S6]. Management's own framing of the last two years is instructive: a large volume gain and a materially lower average selling price of US$48.4/t, a combination that shows how much of the earnings line is benchmark rather than operating [S6].

The domestic leg of the business is a structural feature rather than an afterthought. Roughly 25.7% of tonnes went to Indonesian buyers in the last full year, which places that share of volume under the domestic market obligation regime and its price cap [S6]. The company meets part of that obligation in kind from its lower-cost operations and pays compensation on other volumes, so the economic effect of the cap is diluted but not eliminated [S8]. In the bull scenario it is precisely the domestic share that stops realisations rising as fast as the export marker [S0].

On market position, Bayan is a top-tier Indonesian exporter by volume but not the largest, and its distinctive claim is cost rather than scale [S6]. The company describes its Tabang operations as among the lowest-cost thermal coal mines in the country, and the group-level strip ratio of 4.5x is low for the basin [S6, S8]. Group structure is a holding company over a set of operating subsidiaries, and the controlling shareholder position is currently in flux following a block transfer that section six covers in detail [S2, S10].

Strategy, as the company frames it, is volume growth funded from internally generated cash, continued investment in the Muara Pahu and Tabang barge-loading capacity, and a high dividend payout rather than balance-sheet expansion [S6, S8]. Capex guidance for the current year of a two-to-three hundred million dollar range, against a depreciation charge that is small next to EBITDA, tells the same story: the fleet and the logistics are largely contracted and expensed, so the business converts a large share of EBITDA into cash [S0, S6].

Indonesian thermal coal is an export industry with a domestic obligation grafted on top, and both halves matter to a name like Bayan [S6]. The seaborne market is priced off the Australian and South African markers, but an Indonesian producer's realisation is set by its own calorific value, its ash and sulphur content, the freight differential to the importing market and the tax regime [S6]. The method card is explicit on this point: Indonesian coal names key off the domestic and Indonesian-export indices rather than the Australian marker, and any model that prices them off Newcastle at face value will overstate their revenue [S8].

The demand side is Asia, and increasingly India and South-East Asia rather than China alone [S6]. Chinese policy on domestic mine safety and output, Indian import appetite and the pace of new coal-fired capacity in South-East Asia set the level around which prices oscillate [S6]. Supply is the more interesting half: Indonesian output is administratively gated through the RKAB approval regime, which sets the permitted production plan for each operating entity [S13]. That gate is binding in practice, not in theory — as the current year demonstrated when three Bayan subsidiaries were unable to produce legally pending an approval and declared force majeure to their customers [S13].

The regulatory layer is where the industry-specific risk sits. The domestic market obligation requires producers to supply a share of output to the domestic power market, and the price at which those tonnes are sold has historically been capped well below the export benchmark [S6]. Alongside it, the royalty regime for coal was reworked through the 2025 regulations, and coal royalties now run on two tracks. Producers who took their licences into the new permit form face a stepped, price-linked schedule [S0]. Bayan sits on the contract track: the annual report discloses that the group mines through 5 coal contracts of work, or CCoW, and further IUP licences held by its subsidiaries, and the CCoW note states the Government is entitled to take 13.5% of the coal produced from those five legacy mines, while the IUP licences pay a stepped production fee whose top rate is 11.5% by calorific value and reference-price tier [S6]. What the accounts actually book is the blend of the two — a royalty and production-fee expense of US$269.1m in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — which is why we model a single flat effective rate rather than either headline [S6].

Competitive positioning within the basin is a cost question first and a scale question second [S6]. Bayan's group strip ratio of 4.5x is well inside the Kalimantan norm, and its self-operated hauling and barging chain removes a layer of contractor margin that most peers pay [S8]. The company's own history of low cash costs — US$32.5/t in the last full year against a budget of a materially higher figure — is evidence that the advantage is operational rather than cyclical [S6]. On a cost-curve basis we would place the group in the first quartile of Indonesian thermal producers, which is the moat the method card asks us to identify [S6, S8].

Five-forces, briefly. Supplier power is moderate and rising, because fuel, labour and contracting rates set the cost line and the company named higher fuel prices as the principal driver of its recent cost increase [S8]. Buyer power is low in the export market and high in the domestic market, because the latter is a regulated monopsony [S6]. Substitutes are the long-run threat to thermal coal, and the energy transition is a structural headwind rather than a near-term one [S6]. Rivalry is intense and commoditised, with no pricing power at the individual producer level [S6]. Entry is gated by the licence regime, which cuts both ways: it protects incumbents and it handed three Bayan subsidiaries a production stoppage in the current year [S13].

Our industry complex view, consistent with the desk's neutral stance on thermal coal, is that the observed spot benchmark embeds a war premium that the deck mean-reverts over its forecast horizon [S0]. That is the single assumption that drives most of our valuation gap, and the sensitivity grid in section four shows how the answer moves with it [S0].

Coal-fired generation remains the largest single source of electricity in much of Asia, and
retirements in developed markets have been more than offset by additions in emerging ones. Exporters
compete on delivered cost, and freight, calorific value and ash content decide whether a cargo is
economic in a given market. Governments influence the industry through permitting, royalty regimes
and domestic-supply obligations rather than through direct ownership.

The historical record is one of a high-margin, cash-generative business whose earnings are set by the benchmark rather than by operating leverage. In the last full year the group reported revenue of US$3,427.6m and a net profit to parent of US$767.9m [S0], and the company's own annual report discloses EBITDA of US$1,160.0m on that year [S6]. Our engine models EBITDA of US$1,113.4m — an EBITDA margin of 32.5% — a figure that differs from the disclosed one by a few percent and traces to the depreciation basis rather than to any operating line, since the data pack's D&A for this name is a stub (section below). The prior year was broadly similar at the revenue line, which is the point: volume grew sharply while the realised price fell, so revenue was almost exactly flat year on year [S0, S6].

The cost side is the franchise. Cash costs per tonne came down to US$32.5/t, comfortably inside the prior year's US$37.8/t and well inside the budget for both years [S6, S7]. Our forecast carries that advantage forward rather than fading it, because the drivers are structural — a low strip ratio, the self-operated logistics chain and a weak regional cost base [S6, S8]. The model's unit cost is built bottom-up from the mining block, the hauling and barging block and a royalty line, at a single effective royalty rate of 8% of revenue reconciled to the Company's own disclosed cost stack, where the royalty share of the all-in quarterly cash cost implies under a tenth of revenue at the reported quarterly ASP, against the two full-year histories either side of it [S8, F5, F6]. That reported cost already includes royalty, so the mining blocks are carried ex-royalty and the line is counted once, not twice. On peer comparability, a caveat the cost block requires: unlike some covered coal names we carry a per-tonne cost intensity rather than a physical bcm/t strip ratio in the model, so the 4.5x group strip ratio is context, not the cost driver the multiple axis turns on. The quantity that is comparable across the peer set is the per-tonne cash cost, and on that basis Bayan's mining block sits at or below the covered names once its self-operated hauling and barging chain is allowed for [S8, F7]. On the royalty itself we book the effective rate, not a headline: the group mines under coal contracts of work, or CCoW, as well as IUP licences [S6, F28], the CCoW contract rate is 13.5% and the IUP production fee steps up to 11.5% [S6], but the consolidated royalty and production-fee expense the accounts actually show is US$269.1m against US$3,427.6m of revenue in the last full year and US$263.8m the year before — so the flat 8% of revenue in the model carries the blend the company pays, not the contract ceiling, and the licence base is now stated rather than inferred [S6].

Our forecast volumes start close to the record level of the last full year and then grow modestly into the capacity ramp, and are held flat thereafter rather than faded: the stated JORC reserve base of 2,030 Mt — the 1 April 2022 statement, the company's latest, net of the tonnes mined since — supports roughly two and a half decades at this run-rate, so nothing in the reserve statement or the contracted book sources a decline, and we do not put an unsourced one in [S6, S8]. We are deliberately below management's own target for the current year, because the force-majeure episode and the RKAB timing make the top end of the guided range an aspiration rather than a plan [S13]. The company has, however, contracted a large share of the current year's book at 67.2 Mt, which gives a floor to the volume line even if the price is reset [S8].

Our current-year revenue and profit run above the company's own FY2026 plan, and the gap needs reconciling because it is the price deck rather than the operating plan. Bayan's own FY2026 plan assumes a Newcastle price of 105.0 USD/t and, on that assumption, guides revenue to US$1.8bn to US$3.8bn and EBITDA of US$0.5bn to US$1.0bn [S6]. We carry the group volume inside the guided production range — modelled FY2026E sales of 71.0 Mt — but price it off the sector deck's FY2026E Newcastle marker of US$137/t [S0], which sits above the company's own planning price, so modelled FY2026E revenue of US$4,363.1m and EBITDA of US$1,859.0m land above the top of the guided band. Held at the company's own price plan the forecast would fall back toward it: the difference is the deck's near-year marker, which the method card re-sets whenever the complex moves, not a divergence from the operating plan on volume or cost.

Cash conversion is excellent and is the reason the dividend is credible. Operating cash flow in the last full year was US$501.4m before working-capital swings and capex, capex was US$170.9m, and the balance sheet ended with net debt of US$-574.6m [S0]. That is a genuine negative net-debt figure, not a rounding artefact, and it means the group's net-debt-to-EBITDA is negative in a trough as well as in a peak [S0]. A producer with no leverage and a first-quartile cost position can survive a severe price fall that would force a levered peer into a distressed equity raise, which is exactly the asymmetry the method card wants us to price [S0, S8].

Both the da key and the D&A charge itself are restated from the LK notes rather than the data pack (fixed-asset depreciation of US$111.1m in FY2025 and US$96.6m in FY2024 [S6], sourced in the segment note; the data pack reads under three million). That restatement lifts reported history EBITDA from the pack's understated figure to the one the table shows, because the pack's D&A line is the stub — not the charge. Capital allocation is the clearest signal of management's intent. The company paid US$500 of dividends in respect of the last completed year against a five-year average payout of 73.0%, and it has done so while funding its capacity programme internally [S8]. We model the payout at 73%, held broadly flat, which is a genuine judgement: a lower benchmark with an unchanged payout ratio would cut the dividend materially, and that is the transmission channel between the coal price and the share price [S0, S8].

Earnings quality. We have worked through the methodology's flag list and the picture is unusually clean for the sector. On accruals, the divergence between accounting profit and cash generation is small and stable, with capex and depreciation both low relative to EBITDA and no evidence of capitalised costs masking a cash shortfall [S0]. The related-party screen is not entirely clean, and we state it as we find it, quantified. The group's coal revenue includes a related-party slice of US$185.9m in the last full year, a low-single-digit share of group sales [S6]. The related-party balance sheet is larger than the revenue flow: trade payables to related parties were US$35.2m and trade receivables from them US$12.3m at the last balance-sheet date, and there is a related-party civil-works contract with PT Nirmala Matranusa (NMN) for the Senyiur jetty worth US$51.9m across the 2023-24 fiscal years [S6]. On the accrual screen the picture is the opposite of an aggressive one: the group's operating cash generation exceeds its reported profit, so the accruals ratio is negative — cash is running ahead of accounting earnings rather than behind them — and we find no receivable or inventory build that outruns revenue [S0]. Our verdict is optics-class, not manipulation-class: the flows are disclosed line by line, small against revenue and assets, and the coal is also sold to third-party customers — but the related-party payable is not nothing, and it sits beside the off-market block transfer that section six discusses rather than being waved away [S6]. There is no serial equity issuance, no pledge disclosure of the kind that would impair control, and no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion in the covered period [S6].

Two flags do need stating. First, the group's working-capital position and its receivables profile warrant monitoring, because a producer selling into a regulated domestic market carries a payment-timing risk that export-only peers do not [S0, S6]. Second, the effective royalty and tax lines are policy variables rather than operating ones, and the 2025 coal regulations introduced a stepped royalty schedule that could raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime [S0]. Bayan states it sits outside that regime, but it is a live policy risk and we treat it as such in section five [S8]. Finally, the off-market block transfer that section six discusses is a governance flag rather than an accounting one, and we flag it here because it bears on how an investor should weight the reported earnings stream [S2].

Reported profit for a coal producer is a poor guide to the value of the business, because the price
that produced it will not persist. The cash-conversion question is the important one: how much of
each dollar of earnings survives as free cash after capex and working capital, and how much of that
is returned. A producer that converts earnings into cash and returns it to shareholders is worth
more than the same earnings stream retained in a business with no reinvestment opportunity.

We value Bayan with a life-of-asset discounted cash flow as the primary method, weighted 60% of the target, with an exit-multiple cross-check at 25% and a dividend-yield cross-check at 15% [S0]. The method set fits the industry because the asset is a depleting reserve with a finite life, not a growth business: the method card is explicit that a cyclical producer should never be valued on a single year's earnings, and that the correct frame is the net present value of the cash the reserve will generate at a through-cycle price, less debt and corporate costs [S0, S9].

We build the discount rate from the macro deck rather than from feel. The risk-free rate is 5.0% in dollar terms, the mature-market equity risk premium is 4.2%, and the Indonesian country risk premium adds 2.5%, giving a cost of equity of 11.3% [S0]. We take the equity beta from the industry regression rather than from a subjective judgement, and because the company carries no net debt the gearing adjustment is nil, so the weighted average cost of capital equals the cost of equity at 11.3% [S0]. On top of the regression beta we carry a governance overhang in the base case itself, not only in the bear: a live exchange clarification over the off-market control-block transfer at Rp2,588 against a tape near Rp11,100 [S2, S10] and a September force-majeure stoppage that was outside minority control [S13] justify a small required-return overlay, which is why our cost of equity sits inside rather than below the covered coal peer range. We assume no terminal growth at all, which is deliberate: a depleting thermal-coal asset should not be assigned perpetual real growth, so the value sits in the explicit cash flows rather than in a terminal multiple [S0].

The primary DCF runs over the reserve life implied by the stated JORC reserve base of 2,030 Mt, the company's latest published statement, dated 1 April 2022 and still shown on its Reserve & Resources page [S9, S11]. That base is stale by construction: disclosed production of 56.2 Mt of sales in FY2024 and 68.0 Mt in FY2025, on top of an earlier year of similar scale, has consumed a large slice of it since the statement date, so the effective remaining life is shorter than the headline figure implies, and we run the DCF to the year the reserve depletes rather than into empty tail years. The shortfall is a downside the bear carries, not a base-case haircut. Stated as a sensitivity rather than a haircut: because our horizon already ends at the year the reserve depletes, a reader who marks the headline reserve figure to market would compute a longer life and a higher value than ours, and the difference is simply the tonnes mined since the statement; if a newer JORC statement is published the horizon, and with it the DCF value, moves with it, and we will re-strike it then rather than invent a replacement figure now. At the deck's long-run benchmark, and with the realisation haircut that an Indonesian sub-bituminous producer requires, the modelled average selling price settles near the mid-forties in US dollars a tonne against an all-in cash cost in the low thirties, a margin that is positive but far thinner than the last two reported years [S0, S6]. Discounted at the cost of equity and with no terminal value, that stream supports Rp3,954 a share, and the terminal value share of the total is 0.0% — which is the point of the method, since the entire value is explicit and none of it is a terminal assumption [S0].

The two cross-checks now part company with each other, and honesty requires us to say so rather than to average the disagreement away. The EV/EBITDA cross-check capitalises a normalised EBITDA at 6.5x times — the median of an explicit seaborne-export peer cohort (ADRO, AADI, BSSR, ITMG, PTBA, GEMS, MCOL, INDY), not BYAN's own peak-distorted four-year mean, which was struck when EBITDA was small in the price-war and low-volume years and is shown as the distribution it is in the table, not used as the anchor — and produces Rp3,973 a share, 0.5% versus the primary: the two methods now broadly agree, each capitalising the same forward cash flows. On the basis of the cross-check, one disclosure: the cohort median of 6.5x is the median of the eight-name seaborne set above [S0]; the four names under our own coverage whose latest-year multiples we can see print a lower median, so if the cross-check were struck on that narrower, house-covered subset alone it would land closer to the primary DCF rather than further from it — the cross-check is if anything generous to the share price, not to our target. The dividend-yield cross-check is the outlier. It capitalises the model's own forecast next-twelve-months payout at the cohort's median yield of 8.2%, producing Rp6,465, or 63.5% above the primary [S0]. It uses the model's payout on modelled earnings — which fall as the price normalises — so it is not the pre-cut stream, but capitalising any maintained dividend at a through-cycle yield still reaches a level the depleting reserve cannot fund. In plain terms: our primary method values the coal and the multiple cross-check agrees with it, while the dividend anchor values what the export complex will pay for this class of equity [S0].

None of the three methods reaches the price, and the ordering between them is itself the finding. The reserve DCF and the exit-multiple cross-check now broadly agree, because both capitalise the same forward cash flows; the dividend-yield anchor, which capitalises a payout the depleting reserve cannot fund, sits materially higher and is the only one of the three within reach of the tape [S0]. So the price is not being set by the coal at all — it is being set by the dividend, and the dividend is a function of the benchmark the market assumes persists. If the benchmark normalises toward the deck's long-run path and the payout is maintained, the DCF and the multiple cross-check will look right and the dividend anchor will collapse; if the premium persists indefinitely, the dividend anchor is still short of today's price and the shares are capitalising something none of our methods can see [S0, S6]. Which anchor you believe is the whole investment question, and we take the through-cycle view that the method card prescribes [S0].

The sensitivity grid shows the answer is almost entirely a benchmark question rather than a cost or volume question: a full deck-step change in the price assumption moves the value sharply while the volume and cost-intensity axes move it far less [S0]. One caveat on the exhibit: the IDR/USD axis is inert because Bayan reports and sells in US dollars, so the engine's translation of a USD cash-flow stream back to rupiah takes currency outside the sensitivity — the flat rows are a statement about the functional currency, not evidence that currency does not matter, and we discuss the two-sided translation risk in section five [S0, S8]. That price-taker profile with a fixed cost base is why we spend more of this report on the price deck than on the operating plan [S0].

Before we strike the value we re-checked the balance-sheet date. The last reported balance sheet is 30 June 2026, and nothing after it requires an adjustment to enterprise value: the second-quarter update showed cash of US$954.1m with no net debt and the capex programme intact [S8]; three subsidiaries declared force majeure in September pending the unapproved RKAB revision, after which extra quota was granted [S13, S14]; and the October control-block transfers were made between existing holders, so no cash reached the company [S2, S10]. No divestment, acquisition, special or interim dividend, rights issue, contingent consideration or asset held for sale was disclosed after that date, so the bridge stays empty and the value is struck on the reserve and the contracted book alone [S8, S13].

Finally, the reverse-DCF frame, which asks what the market price implies rather than what we think the price should be. The engine solves it on the nearest fully-market deck year, FY2027E (US$118/t a tonne), so the factor is stated against that marker and not the long-run one: holding our cost and volume assumptions, the current price of Rp10,750 requires the benchmark to average roughly 205 through the forecast horizon, about 1.7 times the deck's FY2027E marker and a larger multiple of the US$105/t long-run marker [S0]. That is above the current spot benchmark, which already embeds a war premium, and it is a demanding assumption to underwrite for a depleting asset [S0]. Note also that the deck's own near-year marker already sits below today's tape, so the required benchmark is above the deck outright rather than merely above a depressed long-run assumption [S0]. Either the premium persists indefinitely, or the shares are capitalising a dividend that a normalising price will not sustain [S0, S8]. We do not think both can be true.

The dominant downside risk is the coal price itself, and it is not a hypothetical. The deck's long-run benchmark is well below the current spot, which means our base case already assumes a substantial decline, and a faster or deeper normalisation would take the shares through our bear value in a single year [S0]. The mechanism is mechanical rather than subtle: a lower benchmark lowers the realised price, compresses the margin against a largely fixed cost base, and cuts the dividend, and the dividend is what the market has been paying for [S8].

The second risk is regulatory and it is specific to Indonesia. The RKAB approval regime gates production legally, and the current year showed that a delay is not a theoretical risk but a live one: three subsidiaries declared force majeure to their customers because they could not produce legally pending an approval [S13]. A repeat, or a lengthening of the approval cycle, hits volume and revenue directly and is outside management's control [S13]. The 2025 royalty regulations are the companion risk on the cost side, since a move into the stepped schedule would raise the cost line for producers in the converted-licence regime; the bear now carries that uplift explicitly, with the effective royalty stepping toward the top IUP rate the annual report quotes [S0, S6, F30]. The same regime can also lift the domestic-market share above the 25.7% we observe — the government is gating total output through RKAB rather than the DMO percentage, so we hold the capped share at its last actual, but a rising obligation would dilute realisation faster than the model allows and is a risk we watch [S6, F10].

The third risk is execution on capacity, though we regard it as the mildest. The barge-loading and camp programme is internally funded and the company has delivered on similar projects before, so the risk is slippage rather than failure [S6, S8]. Currency is a two-sided risk: the group reports in dollars and sells in dollars, so translation risk is limited, but a materially weaker rupiah would raise dollar costs over time even as it flatters reported margins briefly [S0, S8]. Liquidity is a real consideration for an outside investor rather than a fundamental one: the free float is 21.3% of the register, and the controlling block is concentrated, so the shares are liquid only by the standards of a large-cap, not of an index heavyweight [S0].

The fourth risk is governance, and it is the one we carry in the bear rather than leave in the narrative. A control-register transfer at a price far below the market, between parties connected with control, is the kind of event that can hold a trust discount on the register for as long as the ownership is unsettled — the reverse-DCF shows what that costs if the required return rises, and the model encodes it as a higher cost of equity rather than a price shock because a governance overhang changes the discount rate an outside holder demands, not the coal price: the base case carries a small overlay and the bear doubles it [S2, S10].

Thermal-coal producers are exposed to the same broad risks everywhere: price, permitting, cost
inflation and the energy transition. What differs by jurisdiction is who bears the permitting risk
and how the domestic-supply obligation is priced. In Indonesia the state carries the permitting
lever directly, which makes the policy calendar as important to a forecast as the price calendar.

Our scenario weights are 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull, close to symmetric because we see the two tails as genuinely balanced rather than as a skew to protect, and the tails now move the same four drivers (benchmark, volume, required return and royalty) by mirrored or explicitly sourced amounts. The bear is built from four parts, not the price alone. First, the benchmark is taken down a fifth from the deck's through-cycle path — the exact mirror of the bull's step up — which carries it through the marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names [S0]. Second, the RKAB squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume: the September force-majeure declaration by the three subsidiaries [S13] was met by an additional 15 to 20 Mt of 2026 quota the government granted them [S14], so we carry a lasting group-level clip rather than the one-off event's full size, while the unchanged payout cuts the dividend mechanically with the lower price [S13, S14]. Third, the royalty regime tightens: the bears carry the IUP/CCOW conversion risk with the effective royalty stepping up toward the top IUP rate, the schedule the annual report itself quotes [S6, F30]. Fourth, the ownership overhang is carried as a separate governance shock — a higher required return on the register, not a price move — which is how the Jhonlin block shows up in the bear rather than being left out of it [S2, S10]. Together the bear takes the value to Rp1,946 [S13]. The bull case mirrors each step: the premium holds and supply discipline lasts into the following year, so the benchmark runs a fifth above the deck's path; the royalty regime is eased rather than tightened; volumes run a tenth above plan as Bayan's low-cost tonnes take share and the tabang capacity funded by the US$770.0m already spent ramps toward the company's own 80 million tonne target [S6, F33]; and the ownership overhang settling lowers the required return — taking the value to Rp6,087 [S0, S8].

The signposts we will watch are concrete. A sustained move in the benchmark toward the deck's long-run path would validate the primary method and cut the value sharply; a breakdown in the RKAB approval discipline, or a repeat force majeure, would hit volume before it hit price; and any change to the royalty regime would move the cost line in a way the model would have to reflect [S0, S13]. On the other side, a decision by the board to maintain or raise the payout ratio through a price decline would be the strongest possible signal that management sees the downturn as cyclical rather than structural [S8].

Ownership and control are the governance story here, and they moved in the covered period. The largest single shareholder is PT Jhonlin Baratama, which held 30.2% of the issued and paid-up capital as at the most recent ownership report [S10]. Dato' Low Tuck Kwong and Elaine Low together hold a slightly larger block, and the company stated on the basis of control letters that there had been no change of control [S10]. That is the calm version of the story, and it is not the whole story.

The disclosed transfers that prompted the exchange's questions were executed off-market at Rp2,588 a share in the middle of that October and again at Rp2,588 a share the next day, against a Rp11,100 close on the first of those days and a Rp11,200 on-market purchase by Dato' Low Tuck Kwong the day before — so the transfer price is a little under a quarter of the tape, not a "small fraction" of it [S2, S10]. Two facts discipline the reading. First, the price is contractual rather than a discovery: the exchange tied the identical first-day price directly to the pelaksanaan Perjanjian Jual Beli Saham Bersyarat (PJBS), a conditional share purchase agreement, with Jhonlin Baratama, and asked whether a change to that agreement had produced a further transfer [S2]. The buyer is PT Jhonlin Baratama and the sellers are the control-block holders, so this is a transfer between connected parties on a PJBS formula, not a minority price fixed by the market [S10]. Second, the holdings confirm it moved between existing holders rather than off the register: as at the October ownership report Dato' Low Tuck Kwong held 8.3% of the capital, he and Elaine Low together held 30.3%, and PT Jhonlin Baratama held 30.2% as the resulting stake [S2, S10]. We therefore do not claim an unsourced aggregate block; the disclosure supports the per-date prices and the resulting holdings, and no more. The company answered that it was not a party to the transactions and could not confirm their substance, and both it and the ministry denied any link to the RKAB process [S2, S10, S15].

The question this raises for an outside shareholder is about the alignment of the controlling block rather than about disclosure compliance. A transfer at a price far below the market, from or to parties connected with control, is the kind of event that makes the market ask what the transacting parties believe the shares are worth, and it coincided with the RKAB approval process, which the mining ministry publicly stressed was unrelated to the share acquisition [S15]. We note that both the company and the ministry took the trouble to deny a connection, which tells you the connection was being made [S13, S15].

On the rest of the governance file the picture is unremarkable and mostly positive. The dividend record is strong and consistent, with a five-year average payout of 73.0% and a large distribution in respect of the last completed year [S8]. The board and audit arrangements show no flagged issues in the covered filings, there is no auditor downgrade or qualified opinion, and we found no serial equity issuance or pledge disclosure that would impair control [S6]. Related-party revenue is not material to the group's sales, which is the flag the methodology asks us to test and one of the few places where the company scores cleanly [S6].

On ESG, the exposures are the ones intrinsic to thermal coal. The group's emissions are scope one and scope two from mining, hauling and barging plus the much larger scope three from combustion of the coal it sells, and the latter is the material figure for any investor applying a transition lens [S6]. Land rehabilitation and mine-closure obligations are a real long-tail liability for any Kalimantan producer, and the group's reclamation provisioning is a line we will track through the filings [S6]. On the social side, the mining workforce is large and locally concentrated, which creates both licence-to-operate value and community-relations risk [S6]. None of this changes the investment case at the price in question, but a transition-aware buyer should size the position for the scope-three exposure rather than for the reported emissions [S6].

The nearest catalyst is the operating update for the current quarter, which will show whether the force-majeure episode cost volume that the additional quota does not recover, and whether the contracted book of 67.2 Mt is holding [S8, S13]. Alongside it sits the FY2027 RKAB cycle for the three affected subsidiaries, because an orderly approval would remove the single largest operational tail risk in the model and a repeat delay would reprice it [S13].

The dividend decision is the value catalyst, and it is the one the market actually trades. The company's five-year record of a 73.0% payout is the anchor the multiple rests on, and a board decision to maintain or raise the payout through a weakening price would be read as a signal about management's own view of the cycle [S8]. Conversely, a cut would validate the primary valuation method faster than any price move [S0].

We will monitor a short list of indicators between updates. First, the benchmark price path against the deck's assumption, since the sensitivity grid shows it dominates every other variable [S0]. Second, the realised-price spread to the benchmark, because it is the company-specific number that tells us whether the quality discount is widening or narrowing [S6]. Third, unit cash costs against our bottom-up build, with fuel and contracting rates the inputs to watch [S8]. Fourth, the RKAB calendar and any further force-majeure disclosure [S13]. Fifth, and at the governance level, any further disclosure on the Jhonlin Baratama block and the resolution of the exchange's clarification request [S2, S10]. We will revisit the through-cycle marker itself if the complex moves, as the method card requires, rather than assuming the deck stands still [S0].

bear.narrative: The war premium unwinds and overshoots: the bear takes the deck's long-run Newcastle marker down a full 20% (the exact mirror of the bull, the house default), which is a demand-led trough through the US$100-110/t marginal-cost floor the coal deck itself names, and the RKAB quota squeeze persists and clips a twentieth of group volume — the disclosed one-off cure ESDM granted the three affected subsidiaries was larger, an additional 15-20 Mt or about a fifth to a quarter of group output [S14], so the bear carries a lasting residual clip rather than the temporary halt annualised. The new Jhonlin control block is carried as a separate +200bp governance overhang on the required return rather than as a price move, and the lower benchmark with the unchanged 73% payout cuts the dividend mechanically — so the bear value and the dividend cut arrive together, because the dividend is the anchor the market pays for.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same four drivers: the war premium holds and Chinese mine-safety curbs plus RKAB discipline keep seaborne supply tight into 2027, so the benchmark runs 20% above the deck's long-run path; Bayan's low-cost Tabang tonnes take share and volumes run 10% above plan (toward the company's own more-than-80-million-MT-per-annum ramp target) as the Muara Pahu and Tabang capacity, funded by the US$0.77bn of debottlenecking capex already spent, runs full; the royalty regime is eased rather than tightened; and as the ownership overhang settles the required return falls 200bp rather than rises.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: FY2026E is calibrated below management's own target rather than at it: the Company guided 2026 production to "the higher end of the range of between 39-76 million MT" after three subsidiaries (TA, TJ, FSP) declared force majeure on 11 September 2026 because the RKAB 2026 revision was unapproved, and ESDM only then granted the three an additional 15-20 Mt of quota [S6, S13, S14]. We therefore hold FY2026E near the FY2025 actual of 70.8 Mt [F1] with only a modest step-up, then grow to FY2028E as the Muara Pahu/Tabang capacity ramp (45+ Mt of added barge capacity) is used, then held FLAT rather than faded: the group's stated JORC reserve base of 2,030 Mt [F8] supports roughly two and a half decades at this run-rate, so nothing in the reserve statement or the contracted book [F14] sources a decline, and the most-likely policy forbids an unsourced volume fade. The path is capped by JORC reserves in the engine [F8].

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: Bayan realises a deep discount to the Newcastle 6,000 NAR marker: its product is lower-CV sub-bituminous (the 2026 contracted book is priced at an average of 4,088 kcal/kg GAR, S8), a quarter of tonnes go to the domestic market at HBA/DMO-linked prices (25.7% of volume in 2025, F10), and the method card is explicit that Indonesian coal realisation keys off HBA/ICI, not Newcastle. The ratio is calibrated on the LAST completed fiscal year's actuals against the deck series that prices the product, d.coal.newc: FY2025 ASP of US$48.4/MT (F3) over the deck's FY2025A average of US$108.4/MT [d.coal.newc] = 0.446, corroborated by FY2024 at 0.450 (ASP US$61.3/MT, F4, over US$136.1/MT). It is held flat rather than drifted up, because a ratio fitted to a forecast year would carry that year's premium or trough into the long run — which is exactly the error the restated FY2025A deck actual now removes.

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: Near a quarter of Bayan's tonnes go to the Indonesian domestic market (25.7% of volume in 2025, F10) and the Tabang operations meet their Domestic Market Obligation in kind while the higher-CV mines pay DMO compensation, so we place 25% of tonnes under the standing US$70/t power cap carried in the coal deck (d.coal.dmo_cap). Capped tonnes receive min(cap, realised price), which bites hardest in the bull scenario. Why 25% is a level and not a rising ceiling: the DMO is a fixed share of output set by the government (25% of production for domestic supply), and the company's own disclosed domestic share has been stable at 25.7% of volume in the last full year [F10], so we hold the capped share at 25% rather than ramp it. The government is constraining total output through RKAB quotas, not lifting the DMO percentage, so a rising domestic share is a risk we state in §5 rather than a modelled drift.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: Cost intensity is carried as a unit factor rather than a physical bcm/t ratio: the reported cost stack is per-tonne, so the mined ratio (group strip ratio 4.5x based on production volume in 2025, 4.7x in 2Q26, F7) is used as the physical context and the factor below is the per-tonne cost intensity that reproduces the reported unit cost. It drifts up modestly as Tabang's stripping rises off its current low base (Tabang at 3.9x in 2025 against a 4.5x mine plan) and the short-haul coal is exhausted. PEER-COMPARABILITY RECONCILIATION (the AADI/GEMS/BUMI convention books the physical bcm/t ratio in this axis with a cost_per_bcm of US$2.6-8.0/t, so BYAN's unit factor 1.0 is NOT directly comparable): here unit_factor = 1.0 and the axis is a cost-intensity multiplier, so strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm = 1.0 x US$22.0/t is the mining-block cost per tonne, which equals the peer-implied mining cost per tonne (AADI 4.35 bcm/t x US$4.3/t ≈ US$18.7/t; BUMI 8.0 x US$2.6 ≈ US$20.8/t) once BYAN's self-operated logistics and lower physical ratio are allowed for — i.e. the per-tonne cash cost is the comparable quantity, not the axis value. The group's physical strip ratio of 4.5x [F7] is disclosed as context in §1 and §3.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: Mining cost per tonne ex-royalty. Backed out of the reported cash cost and the presentation's own 2Q26 cost stack (overburden and mining 39%, coal hauling 19%, barging 13%, employee 9%, other production 6%, SGA 2%, royalty 12% of a US$37.0/MT all-in cost, S8): ex-royalty cash cost of about US$32.6/MT at 2Q26 and US$28.6/MT at the FY2025 all-in cost of US$32.5/MT (F5). We carry about US$22-23/t for the overburden-mining and coal-hauling block (the 39% overburden and mining plus part of the 19% coal-hauling share of the stack) and put the balance in other_cost_unit, so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm + other_cost_unit + royalty reproduces the reported all-in unit cost. It drifts up moderately as Tabang's stripping rises off a low base. Fuel is passed through the deck's Brent path.

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: Residual per-tonne cost after the royalty and the mining block: employee, other production, SGA and contingency, plus the small non-coal cost base. Set so that the modelled FY2026E unit cost plus royalty lines up with the FY2025 realised all-in cash cost of US$32.5/MT (F5) and the 1H26 run-rate, and inflated gently with wage and services cost thereafter. This is where the barging, employee and SGA shares of the 2Q26 cost stack sit, so it is larger than the mining block per tonne at Tabang's current stripping.

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Restated from the LK notes, not the data pack: Bayan's consolidated fixed-asset depreciation is US$111.1m for FY2025 (F22) and US$96.6m for FY2024 (F23) per the segment note, i.e. US$1.57/t on FY2025 sales of 70.8 Mt (and US$1.72/t on FY2024's 56.2 Mt) — the pack's US$2.0m D&A is a stub because the IDX cash-flow statement uses the direct method and carries no D&A add-back. Mining- property amortisation (US$10.5m FY2025, US$6.4m FY2024) is not added separately: it is already inside the reported cash cost the unit-cost build reconciles to, so counting it here would double-count. Held at the FY2025A rate of US$1.57/t thereafter, with the fleet contracted and expensed through the cash-cost line.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: Sustaining capex only. Bayan guided 2026 capex to US$200-300 million (S6) against FY2025 capex of about US$171m (S0), which on ~71 Mt is roughly US$3/t; part of that is discretionary growth (the fourth Muara Pahu barge loader, BCT upgrade) and is carried separately in capex_other, so the per-tonne sustaining figure is set below the guided average. Held FLAT in real terms thereafter — the series escalates with the macro deck's US long-run inflation, so there is no real drift; the most-likely policy holds costs at the last actual in real terms and nothing in the filings sources a real rise in sustaining capex per tonne.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: Discretionary expansion capex, the balance of the guided US$200-300m 2026 programme (S6): the fourth barge loader at Muara Pahu and the BCT and FSP camp works. Held near the guided run-rate for the first three years, then stepped down as the Tabang capacity programme completes; the buoyant case in §4 adds nothing here because the capacity is already funded.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Payout is the company's own five-year record: 73% of NPAT for 2021-2025 (F12), with US$700m paid in respect of 2024 and US$500m in respect of 2025 (F11) against a net-cash balance sheet and no debt. We hold 73% rather than the engine's three-year average, which is skewed by the extraordinary FY2022-FY2023 cycle, and treat the dividend as the anchor the market prices.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: The primary DCF runs to the end of the reserve life with no terminal value, so this input only feeds the cross-checks (EV/EBITDA and the implied multiple frame). It is set at the house cap for a USD-reporting name, below long-run US inflation, because a thermal-coal cash flow stream should not be assigned perpetual real growth.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Bayan runs a lean corporate cost base: SG&A has averaged under 3% of revenue over FY2023-FY2025 in the data pack (S0). Held near the historical average, drifting up slightly as corporate and ESG costs grow.

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat regimes)
assumptions.basis: Effective royalty of 8% of revenue, derived bottom-up from the Company's own disclosed cost stack rather than from the IUPK parent rate: in the 2Q26 presentation royalty is 12% of a US$37.0/MT all-in cash cost (US$4.4/MT) against a US$58.1/MT ASP, i.e. 7.6% of revenue, and the same arithmetic on FY2025 (12% of US$32.5/MT on a US$48.4/MT ASP) gives 8.1% (S8, F5). We use a flat 8% because Bayan is not an ex-PKP2B IUPK converter and so sits outside the IUPK step schedule, and the presentation states its rates are "lower royalty rates than IUPK's" (S8). The 2025 royalty regime change (PP 18/2025, PP 19/2025) is a live policy risk carried in §5. The deck's reviewed IUPK step table (coal.royalty_iupk) applies only to ex-PKP2B continuation holders (KPC, Arutmin, Berau, MHU, Kendilo, AADI) and so is not read for Bayan; the deck's IUP calorie table (coal.royalty_iup) is needs_source, so the regime cannot be tilted against Bayan on that basis. Double-count check: royalty is already INSIDE the reported US$32.5/MT cash cost (F5's label reads "incl. royalty"), so the mining block and other_cost_unit are set EX-ROYALTY (cost_per_bcm 22.0 + other_cost_unit 5.5 = US$27.5/MT, against the ex-royalty US$28.6/MT implied by stripping 12% of US$32.5), and the engine adds royalty back as a separate % of revenue — so the line is counted once, not twice.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: Fuel is a real cost pressure — the Company named higher fuel prices as the main driver of the 2Q26 cash-cost increase (S8) — but most of Bayan's mining, hauling and barging is contracted to third parties at unit rates that already embed their diesel cost, so only a minority of the cost base is directly fuel-exposed. We set 10% rather than the 30% template convention, and give the reason: the oil deck's long-run Brent is a seeded, war-premium value, and passing a perpetual war premium through the mining cost while the coal deck mean-reverts toward US$105/t would manufacture a margin squeeze that neither deck actually asserts.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: Non-coal revenue (the small oil-palm and services lines) was about US$20m in 2025 (S6); carried flat rather than grown, as it is immaterial to value.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: Template constant 10%; the non-coal lines are immaterial to group value.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: Bayan has carried no net debt since 1Q 2021 and had no outstanding loans at the last reported balance sheet, with US$650m of undrawn working-capital facilities (S8); we assume no new borrowing across the forecast.

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Bayan's non-operating line is dominated by interest income on its net-cash balance, which the engine computes separately via cash_yield; no separate non-operating items assumed.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Share count is fixed at the reported 33,333,335,000 shares; no issuance or buyback assumed. The October 2026 block transfer moved ownership between existing holders and changes no share count (S10).

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history: the three-year average of net working capital over revenue in the data pack (S0). Bayan runs a negative-to-thin working-capital position because coal is largely pre-sold, so this is a small drag and is held flat.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: Engine default carried from history: the three-year average effective tax rate in the data pack (S0), close to the 22% Indonesian statutory rate. Held flat; a lower realised price would not change the statutory rate.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: Bayan is debt-free with no drawn facilities (S8), so the cost of debt is not a value driver; the engine default from the thin historical interest expense line is carried unchanged.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0). Cross-checked against the disclosed treasury holdings: Bayan subscribed IDR3tn (US$180m) of Patriot Bonds at a 2% coupon in October 2025 and holds a large net-cash balance (S8), so a low-single-digit yield is consistent.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Engine default from history (S0): minority interests take a small low-single-digit share of net profit, consistent with the reported minority balance sheet interest.

challenges.challenge: The reverse DCF level is stated as ~US$216/t in the qc_justifications extreme_call but ~US$197/t in the investment summary. Both cannot hold; neither shows workings.
challenges.answer: Single number now, taken from the engine and shown in both places: the reverse-DCF target is d.coal.newc solved on the nearest fully-market year, FY2027E, and the current price implies a horizon-average benchmark of US$205/t, a factor of ~1.73 on that year's US$118/t marker (204.7 = 1.735 x 118). The old US$216/t (1.83x) was a stale run; the qc_justifications extreme_call now reads US$205/t / 1.73x, and the report text renders the same value through {{rev.implied_value|num0}} and {{rev.factor}}, so the two cannot diverge again.

challenges.challenge: F8 carries 2,030 Mt JORC reserves as FY2025A, but S9 dates the statement to 1 Jan 2021 / 1 Apr 2022, since when the company has mined roughly 250 Mt (FY2022 partial, FY2024 56.2 Mt sales, FY2025 68 Mt production). The 30-year mine life underpinning dcf_life is therefore overstated by ~3-4 years.
challenges.answer: No newer JORC statement exists — the company's Reserve & Resources page still carries the 1 Apr 2022 RPM statement [S11] — so we do not invent a replacement figure, but we stop presenting it as a FY2025A fact and we stop running the DCF past depletion. F8 is re-labelled FY2022A (the true statement date) and a carry-forward fact F38 at FY2025A feeds the engine; the horizon is cut from 32 to 28 years so the life-of-asset DCF ends at the year the reserve depletes (FY2053E) rather than booking zero-volume tail years, which also clears the capex.long_run gate. Production since the statement (FY2023/FY2024/FY2025) has consumed roughly 200 Mt, so the effective life is nearer 26 years than 30; the shortfall is stated in §4 and carried by the bear rather than left implicit.

challenges.challenge: The 8% flat royalty assumes the five CCoWs stay on the 13.5%-of-production contract track forever, but conversion to IUPK would invoke the stepped schedule the same note quotes (top 11.5%, pinned house table up to 28%). The bear case shocks price, volume and COE but never royalty.
challenges.answer: The royalty line is now shocked in both tails, mirrored: the bear adds +3.5pp to the effective rate (8% -> 11.5%, the top IUP production-fee rate the annual report itself quotes [S6, F30]), stepping the blend toward the converted-licence schedule; the bull eases it by the same 3.5pp. This is the value impact of the IUP mix moving to 11.5%+ carried explicitly in the scenario grid rather than left in the narrative, and it is disclosed in §5. The base rate stays the LK's effective 8% because that is what the accounts show being paid.

challenges.challenge: The bull shocks newc x1.2 off the deck long-run path, which still lands FY2027E near US$142/t — below today's spot of US$150.35 (deck brief). A bull case weaker than the observable tape understates the war-premium-persistence upside the desk itself flags.
challenges.answer: The bull is stated against the deck's through-cycle path, not against today's spot, so the x1.2 shock is the correct mirror of the bear's x0.8 and must not be sized to span a price the desk itself calls a war-premium print it mean-reverts [S0]. Sizing the bull to spot would embed the premium as permanent in the upside case and break the mirrored-shock rule the house method card requires for every coverage packet. The bull is not, however, weaker than the tape in value terms after the other corrections: it now also carries a +10% volume ramp toward the company's own 80 mtpa target [S6, F33] and a royalty-regime easing, so the bull scenario value sits well above the base and is the strongest of the three. The upside is real; it just is not defined off a spot the desk expects to normalise.

challenges.challenge: The chairman guides toward 80 mtpa and S6 discloses US$0.77bn of Tabang debottlenecking capex in four years, yet the bull allows only +5% volume and the base is flat at ~73 Mt for 30 years. The growth option created by that sunk capex is unpriced.
challenges.answer: The bull's volume shock is raised from x1.05 to x1.10, carrying the modelled path (FY2027E 73 Mt) to ~80 Mt — the company's own stated "ramp up to more than 80 million MT per annum" after the Tabang programme [S6, F33], funded by the US$0.77bn of debottlenecking capex already spent [S6, F34]. flags.message: a.volume: bear 0.95 vs bull 1.1 is lopsided — mirror the shock or justify the asymmetry
flags.justification: The volume shock is asymmetric (bear x0.95, bull x1.10) and each leg is sourced. The bull leg carries the company's own stated plan — a "ramp up to more than 80 million MT per annum" after the Tabang debottlenecking [S6, F33], funded by the US$0.77 billion of infrastructure already spent [S6, F34] — so 73 Mt x1.10 = 80.3 Mt reaches that target, and a x1.05 bull would leave the stated capacity unpriced, which the most-likely standard forbids. The bear leg is NOT the disclosed force-majeure scale: S13 discloses only the fact of the declaration (TA, TJ and FSP declared force majeure on 11 September 2026) and carries no percentage and no tonne figure. The disclosed quantum sits in S14, where ESDM granted those three subsidiaries an ADDITIONAL 15-20 Mt of 2026 quota after the halt — roughly a fifth to a quarter of group volume — and that is a temporary, quota-cured interruption of a minority of group output rather than a permanent group-level volume. The bear therefore carries a 5% persistent clip against the RKAB process (the residual risk that the approval cycle bites again), not the full one-off event annualised: carrying 21-28% of volume across the life-of-asset horizon would be an unsourced structural decline of exactly the kind the most-likely rule forbids. The upside is larger because the company's own plan is larger; the downside is bounded because the disclosed shock was cured within the quarter that produced it.

The price implies the sustained war premium, the low-yield dividend capitalisation and a governance premium of zero all persist indefinitely.
